title: Learning Rate Decay Can Exponentially Accelerate SGD for Global Optimization of Nonconvex Functions
claim: Fixed large steps explore but never settle, fixed small steps get trapped locally, while decaying the step size reaches the global optimum.
layout: 2 rows by 3 columns; trajectories on top, 3D histograms below, shared legend
description: A 2×3 grid compares SGD on a toy 2-D nonconvex landscape with four minima: one global (red star) and three local (red circles). The top row shows contour maps with trajectories colored by iteration (purple to yellow). The columns are large fixed noise, small fixed noise and annealed noise. Large noise wanders everywhere. Small noise stays stuck near a local minimum, with a zoomed inset. Annealed noise explores early, then settles at the global minimum. A shared legend marks global min, local min, start and end. The bottom row shows 3D bar histograms of visited locations. The large-noise histogram is diffuse, the small-noise one is a spike at a local minimum, and the annealed one is concentrated at the global minimum. Red labels mark the minima.
caption: The trajectories of the SGD algorithm with fixed large and small step sizes (Columns 1 and 2, respectively) and a decaying learning rate on a toy problem. While a large step size allows the algorithm to explore the landscape efficiently, the small step size causes the algorithm to be trapped in a local minimum, leading to exponential runtime. The decaying step size allows the algorithm to visit the global minimum with high probability in polynomial time (Column 3).
abstract: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is a workhorse algorithm for continuous optimization. It is a folk belief among deep learning practitioners that learning rate decay in SGD substantially improves performance. However, it has remained unclear whether learning rate decay offers an asymptotic advantage for global nonconvex optimization. We answer this question in the affirmative by demonstrating a natural class of nonconvex functions for which, we prove that SGD with learning rate decay requires exponentially fewer gradient queries for global optimization than SGD with any fixed learning rate in the small-step size regime. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first exponential advantage that has been demonstrated for learning rate decay. The class of functions we consider includes many popular benchmark nonconvex functions. Our results provide a robust explanatory theory for the empirically observed benefits of learning rate decay for global optimization. We show that annealing performs the non-logconcave sampling task associated to the optimization problem in polynomial time, via a novel application of weak PoincarÃ© inequalities.
